episodes.213434: Higher moisture across southeast New Mexico on Independence Day resulted in the development of scattered strong to severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. Decaying thunderstorms late in the evening resulted in two brief severe wind gusts at a mesonet station near Dora. episodes.213444: A stationary front stationed across central Pennsylvania allowed for a lifting mechanism for showers and storms during the morning and afternoon hours of July 5, 2026. Showers and isolated thunderstorms began to develop across portions of western and central Pennsylvaia during the late morning hours and began to exhibit slow forward motion and instances of training. This continued into the afternoon and evening hours, where heavy rainfall persisted over Tyrone in Blair County for upwards of an hour. This prompted considerable flash flooding in the borough, with multiple homes being flooded and some roadways taking on between two and three feet of water. There were also two children that were rescued from flood waters near the paper mill in Tyrone due to the flooding. Given the unstable airmass, thunderstorms continued to grow upscale throughout the afternoon and evening hours, producing multiple instances of tree damage across Centre, Mifflin and Franklin Counties. As storms shifted eastward, favorable low-level shear allowed for some storms to form into a line with some areas of rotation, one of which prompted the Lambs Gap EF-1 Tornado in Perry County. This line continued to move eastward and produced multiple instances of wind damage and flash flooding in Cumberland, Dauphin, and Lancaster Counties throughout the evening before shifting east of the region.

While most of the hail was quarter sized, golf-ball hail was observed by a resident 15 miles west northwest of Polo. episodes.213808: A small microburst on July 5 in Eclectic in Elmore County blew trees down around town. The next afternoon, lightning struck a home in Northport in Tuscaloosa County, resulting in an injury.
episodes.213946: A weak surface outflow boundary associated with overnight storms in Kansas moved through the combined Panhandles and stalled just to the south of Amarillo. This allowed for a late start to any diurnal showers and thunderstorms to occur across the region as drier air was in place, limiting storm development. As this drier air moved out of the region by late afternoon, another surface boundary was located around the Highway 60 corridor. This, along with the more southern boundary, was the focus for storm development. Storms developed during the late afternoon and some became strong to severe with hail and damaging winds being observed across portions of the Panhandle, especially in locations along and south of the Highway 60 corridor. These storms were also efficient rain-producers with heavy rainfall occurring that led to some flash flooding in the area.
episodes.214114: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and northern Oklahoma during the early evening of the 4th, along and ahead of a cold front moving into the area. The thunderstorms organized into a squall line as they moved into northeastern Oklahoma during the evening. The atmosphere across eastern Oklahoma became extremely unstable ahead of the thunderstorms, and supported strong downbursts. Numerous damaging wind events and isolated large hail up to quarter size occurred as these storms moved through northeastern Oklahoma.
episodes.214135: Showers and thunderstorms developed in a warm and unstable airmass ahead of a slow moving cold front.
episodes.214183: Hot temperatures on the afternoon of the fifth and a residual outflow boundary from previous day's convection generated scattered thunderstorms from the Rolling Plains into the extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle. Areas off the caprock saw thunderstorms produce large hail with a sufficient amount of deep layer shear in the atmosphere to create somewhat organized convection. Farther west in the southwestern Texas Panhandle, a much drier sub-cloud layer caused one storm to generate severe winds causing wind damage to an irrigation pivot system in Parmer County.
episodes.214190: An inland trough of low pressure and cold front produced a few thunderstorms over the region during the evening hours. One isolated storm became severe and produced wind damage.
episodes.214251: A frontal boundary settled into the area early on July 5th. Weak low pressure developed along this front and moved into Northwest Ohio the morning of July 5th. This low pressure then remained nearly stationary through the 5th and into the 6th before weakening and exiting to the southeast later on the 6th into the 7th. The front and low pressure combined with a weak trough aloft to encourage periods of showers and thunderstorms from the 5th through the 6th. A warm and very humid airmass combined with weak steering flow to support slow-moving thunderstorms with torrential rainfall rates. There were a few different waves of thunderstorms with heavy rain. An initial batch of thunderstorms tracked across northern Ohio during the morning and early afternoon of the 5th, bringing flash flooding and severe weather to the Youngstown area. An EF-1 tornado and macroburst caused extensive wind damage across Mahoning County, leading to widespread power outages and a state of emergency declaration. Additional thunderstorms the evening of the 5th brought flash flooding across North Central Ohio. Lake enhanced showers and thunderstorms developed over Lake Erie overnight July 5th into the 6th, with east-northeast winds pushing this activity towards the western lakeshore. The most notable impacts came on Kelleys Island, where 10 to 15 inches of rain fell over a several hour period and led to significant flash flooding during the early morning hours of the 6th. Additional flooding occurred later in the morning and into the afternoon on the mainland from just south of Toledo to the Port Clinton area, with more storms developing during the afternoon and causing flash flooding east of Cleveland in parts of Lake and Geauga Counties.
episodes.214548: Scattered thunderstorms tracked across northeast Colorado on the 4th. A storm in Washington County briefly became severe with hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter.
episodes.214674: A shortwave trough stationed across Kentucky and a belt of moderate mid-level westerly flow across the Ohio Valley into the Mid Atlantic allowed for ample lift as it continued to move easterly towards western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours of July 4, 2026. Ample instability (with surface-based CAPE in the 2000-3000 J/kg range and DCAPE values between 800-1400 J/kg) ahead of these features with ample moisture given southerly flow allowed for some showers and thunderstorms to begin forming during the mid-afternoon hours. Initially across the northwest, storms were able to sustain themselves based on marginally sufficient shear, with bulk shear in the 20-30 knot range. This allowed for a cluster of thunderstorms to form in Warren County and continue tracking east-southeastward into Lycoming and Sullivan Counties, producing multiple instances of tree damage along with a garage roof being blown off on Sunrise Ridge Road in Potter County. Progressing into the evening hours, thunderstorm development became more numerous with multiple clusters of severe thunderstorms tapping into the very unstable, moist air mass available across central Pennsylvania. One cluster of storms began to form across western Pennsylvania that began to track across the central mountains of central Pennsylvania and into the Middle Susquehanna Valley, producing multiple instances of tree damage with considerable tree damage observed near Sunbury in Northumberland County. The third, and most notable cluster of storms formed on the border between Maryland and Pennsylvania in Bedford County and grew upscale rapidly given the increased moisture coming off of the Chesapeake under southeasterly flow. As this storm progressed eastward, it produced scattered instances of tree damage in Bedford, Fulton, Franklin, and Huntingdon Counties during the evening hours. As this storm moved into the Lower Susquehanna Valley, numerous reports of considerable tree damage was observed in Cumberland, Dauphin, Lebanon, York, and Lancaster Counties. This included multiple swaths of trees down, a steeple of a church ripped off in Cumberland County, and a downburst in Lancaster County. This storm also caused a tree to fall on a tent of a family camping at the Mountain Creek Campground for Independence Day Weekend, resulting in two fatalities and one injury.

episodes.215895: In the wake of a multi-day heat wave, severe thunderstorms crossed portions of eastern New York during the afternoon and early evening hours on July 4, 2026 ahead of a cold front. These storms produced widespread wind damage across southern Columbia, Ulster and Dutchess counties due to downed trees and power lines. ||The Dutchess County 911 Communications Center noted more than 740 calls in a four-hour period during and after the storms with the majority of these noting downed trees and wires. Dutchess County Emergency Management noted that the most significant impacts from these severe thunderstorms occurred in the City and Town of Poughkeepsie, East Fishkill, Hyde Park, LaGrange, Beekman, Union Vale and the Village and Town of Pawling. In Pawling, downed trees and a transformer explosion resulted in a fire that consumed the local CVS Pharmacy and nearby yoga studio. Approximately 41,000 customers lost power in Dutchess County with about 13,000 customers without power in Ulster County. Some of these customers were without power for days due to the extensive cleanup needed before power could be restored. Dry ice and bottled water stations were opened to assist residents without power.
episodes.215938: An impactful round of severe thunderstorms occurred during the late afternoon and evening of the July 4th Holiday across northern and central Oklahoma. Initial thunderstorm clusters produced sporadic large hail and wind damage across northern Oklahoma, especially in Noble and Payne Counties. Later in the evening, strong outflow boundaries (with associated intense thunderstorm activity) merged across/near the Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area. The resultant more organized thunderstorm line went on to produce a significant corridor of damaging winds across the southwestern Oklahoma City area, Moore, Norman and Noble. This included several measured wind gusts of 75-95 mph. Similar events (in type of damage, space and time) from the city of Norman included in this episode are combined. Thus, events included likely do not capture the full scope of damage across the city of Norman.

Shear again remained weaker at less than 30 knots effective, and DCAPE was lower than the previous two days, but sufficient instability with 1000-2000 J/kg of MLCAPE supported some downed trees from damaging wind within the stronger clusters of storms. Efficient rain rates also lead to flash flooding across portions western Pennsylvania with portions of Butler, Jefferson and Clarion counties hit particularly hard. Slippery Rock Borough declared a disaster emergency with several homes experiencing flooded basements and roadway flooding throughout the borough.

episodes.216509: Active weather stretched through the Independence Day weekend amid oppressive heat and tropical moisture, leading to daily showers and thunderstorms across West Virginia. High pressure initially over the region began to condense on July 3rd, which allowed for isolated storms to form along the higher terrain. Coverage then grew in earnest on the 4th of July and then again on the 5th as convective temperatures were breached in the afternoon and scattered storms formed across the state. Storms materialized just before noon across the Kanawha Valley each day and slowly traveled eastward, causing tree and power line damage in its path. The slow movement of these storms also imposed localized flash flooding by July 5th, causing flooded roadways across parts of Boone and Logan Counties. Storms were tied to daytime heating and quickly lost composure after sunset each night as a result, bringing the severe and flooding risks to an end.
episodes.216513: The Independence Day holiday weekend featured an ongoing heat wave, coupled with daily chance of showers and thunderstorms. Precipitation chances increased with each passing day as departing high pressure lost influence over the area. Strong daytime heating and tropical moisture ushering into the region helped to support quick developing storms during the afternoons, which faded with the loss of daytime heating each evening. In southeast Ohio, main implications from these storms were the strong winds that produced tree and power line damage on both July 4th and 5th.
episodes.216514: A nearly stationary frontal boundary was stretched across the northern tier of PA and southern Catskills within a very moist atmosphere with light winds aloft, setting the stage for some slow-moving, heavy showers and embedded thunderstorms during the afternoon and night of Sunday, the 5th and isolated instances of flooding.
episodes.216609: A weakness in the ridge aloft and the presence of a remnant outflow boundary (a result of decaying convection across Oklahoma) led to scattered thunderstorms during the afternoons of July 5th and 6th. episodes.216614: A very hot and humid airmass in place on July 5 resulted in scattered afternoon storms across central Virginia. Given weak flow aloft, these storms were slow-moving and produced locally heavy rain and instances of flash flooding.
episodes.216711: Substantial instability developed during peak heating on July 5, 2026 with MLCAPE values around 2500 J/kg.  Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon. The instability combined with around 20 kts of effective shear supported a few severe storms with damaging winds. Precipitable water values around 2 inches resulted in locally heavy rainfall that produced isolated flash flooding.
episodes.216752: A weak upper-level disturbance moved through the Lower Mississippi Valley on July 5th and was followed by a larger, slow-moving upper trough that remained near the region through July 8. The initial disturbance increased column moisture and thunderstorm coverage. With abundant moisture, strong summertime instability and some drier air in the mid levels, numerous thunderstorms produced both very heavy rainfall and localized damaging downburst winds.
episodes.216753: A weak upper-level disturbance moved through the Lower Mississippi Valley on July 5th and was followed by a larger, slow-moving upper trough that remained near the region through July 8. episodes.216817: A weak upper level trough drifted southeast across Southwest Arkansas and Northcentral Louisiana during the afternoon and evening of July 4th, between two upper level ridges of high pressure anchored over the Rockies/Plains and the Eastern Seaboard. This weakness aloft contributed to adequate large scale forcing, especially when aided by strong daytime heating and ample moisture available. Thus, scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and early evening over portions of Southwest Arkansas and North-central Louisiana, which produced locally damaging winds which downed trees and power lines, as well as locally heavy rainfall which resulted in localized flash flooding in Western Ouachita Parish.
episodes.216823: A weakening Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) moved southeast into Northeast Texas during the early morning hours of July 5th, along a weak upper level disturbance aloft that drifted southeast into East Texas in the northwest flow aloft. While these storms dissipated by daybreak, they produced a large outflow boundary that propagated southeast to near and south of the I-20 corridor by afternoon, with strong heating, ample low level moisture, and resultant instability contributing to additional scattered showers and thunderstorms across this area of East Texas by mid and late afternoon. Some of these storms did become severe, with reports of damaging winds, hail, and isolated instances of localized flash flooding, before weakening during the early evening.
episodes.216866: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the Big Country and Concho Valley. Some of the storms were severe and mainly produced wind damage.

episodes.217000: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms were observed across central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours on July 4th as a typical summertime hot and humid environment was in place across the Ohio Valley. On both days, synoptic forcing was weak across the region with baggy mid- and upper-level troughing and no discernible surface boundaries present. Still, with smaller scale boundaries and an unstable environment in place, pulse thunderstorms were able to develop on July 3rd, with a few downbursts producing wind damage across western Kentucky and southwest Indiana. On July 4th, the remnants of an upstream convective system moved into central Kentucky during the evening hours. While most convection was sub-severe, one particularly strong cell produced isolated wind damage as it moved across Metcalfe and Green County.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey team has determined that a macroburst with straight-line damage of 90 mph occurred in Mahoning County on July 5, 2026, extending for over 10 miles with a path width of over 3 miles. As the EF-1 tornado cycled out across the region, a significant rear flank downdraft formed and increased in intensity, causing substantial straight-line wind damage across a larger portion of Mahoning County. Winds up to 90 mph caused extensive tree, power pole, and power line damage across Austintown Township, Canfield Township, Boardman, and Poland. This phenomenon is called a macroburst and extended for over 10.25 miles and had a maximum path width of 3.3 miles. The macroburst formed on the southwest side of Austintown Township just before 2 PM and proceeded southeast through Mahoning County until after 2:30 PM. The most intense portion of the macroburst was in Canfield Township and Boardman where extensive tree and power line damage was noted east of Ohio State Route 11 to Market Street and along and north of US Route 224. Based on ground and aerial survey footage, it is estimated that nearly a thousand trees were downed across the area. Some trees came down onto area residences, causing roof and siding damage, and some trees toppled onto vehicles, completely destroying them. Damage across the region displayed a clear divergent pattern within the macroburst with trees favoring a southeast wind direction across the general region. While the damage is best described as a macroburst, the 90 mph estimated maximum wind gust intensity is the equivalent of a low-end EF 1 tornado.

A National Weather Service Storm Survey team has determined that a very short-lived EF-1 tornado with winds of 95 mph occurred in Canfield Township on July 5, 2026. The tornado formed in the vicinity of Mellinger Road, where the tops of trees were shredded and thrown onto nearby residences. The tornado continued southeast across US 62, where the tornado toppled more trees and snapped several at their bases with some slight convergent motion. One large tree fell onto a residence severely damaging the home. The tornado continued southeast toward Messerly Road where more tree tops were shredded before the tornado cycled out. This short-lived EF-1 tornado had estimated maximum wind gusts of 95 mph in northeast Canfield Township and was on the ground for about a minute.
